question: Did motorist fatality risk per mile driven in NYC decrease from 2013 to 2025? Create a chart and answer using this crash dataset.

options.reason: Annual counts directly show how the number of motorist deaths recorded in crashes changed over time without adding a substitute exposure denominator.
options.answer: This dataset cannot determine per-mile risk; recorded motorist fatalities fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025, a 26.4% decrease.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether the annual number of motorist deaths recorded in NYC crashes declined: it went down between the endpoints, despite substantial year-to-year variation. It is defensible as a direct count of fatalities in the crash records, but it does not measure risk per mile or adjust for travel volume.

options.denominator: All police-reported crashes in the same calendar year
options.reason: Normalizing fatalities by crash-record volume provides a defensible within-dataset comparison when mileage exposure is unavailable.
options.answer: This dataset cannot determine per-mile risk; fatalities per 100,000 reported crashes rose from 54.0 in 2013 to 94.7 in 2025, a 75.4% increase.
options.interpretation: This framing answers how motorist fatalities compare with the number of police-reported crashes, and the endpoint rate is higher in 2025 than in 2013. It is defensible as a crash-normalized measure using available data, but crashes are not miles driven, so it leaves per-mile fatality risk unanswered.

answer:
The dataset cannot establish whether motorist fatality risk per mile decreased; annual motorist fatalities fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26.4%).
Per 100,000 reported crashes, motorist fatalities rose from 54.0 in 2013 to 94.7 in 2025 (75.4%); this crash-normalized measure does not show per-mile risk.
